newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan town votes down waste plant, others to follow.
newsitem.headline: Japan town votes down waste plant, others to follow.

text.p: A landmark referendum in which residents of a central Japanese town decried plans to build an industrial waste disposal plant was likely to be copied by other municipalities in Japan, officials said on Monday.

In Sunday's vote in Mitake in central Gifu Prefecture, the nation's first ever referendum on an industrial waste plant project, 87.5 percent of the town's voters turned out and opponents outnumbered supporters 10,373 to 2,442.

The rejection in the nonbinding referendum of the industrial waste plant, which local officials planned without informing citizens, was expected to deal a blow to other such schemes throughout Japan, where officials say landfills will reach capacity in two years.

In response to the Mitake vote, officials of Kobayashi city in southwestern Japan said they would hold a vote as early as the end of October on whether to continue construction on a planned industrial waste disposal plant.
A central government spokesman said the referendum result showed Japan "must seriously tackle the issue of industrial waste by making efforts to curb waste and increase recycling".
Mitake and Kobayashi are among more than 100 Japanese municipalities where there are controversies over waste dump plans, according to Health Ministry estimates.

The Mitake case showed popular demand for environmental assessment, government transparency and respect for the democratic process, the liberal daily Asahi Shimbun said in an editorial on the referendum.

Mitake Mayor Yoshiro Yanagawa, elected on a pledge to overturn the scheme, which had been agreed to by his predecessor, was badly beaten up by thugs last October, one month after he asked the prefectural government to freeze construction plans.
Yanagawa's assailants, widely believed to be supporters of the industrial waste plant, were never apprehended.

Sunday's referendum was the third such plebiscite in Japan, following polls last year in the northern Japan village of Maki over nuclear power plant construction and in Okinawa, Japan's southernmost prefecture, over U.S. military bases.

Both those votes, in which voters came out strongly against government policies, were seen as harbingers for the future of politics in a country where voter turnout in elections and confidence in politicians, as expressed in opinion polls, have declined steadily.
